passage:
Dear Nikita,
Thank you for staying late on Friday. I keep thinking about the poster row. Someone in our group wanted to write that the registrar “doesn’t care about students.” I said no, and I checked the timetable myself. The library closes at eight because of the electricity contract, not laziness. So we changed the slogan to what is true: students need it open till eleven in exam weeks.
When Mr. Kulkarni from the office came to our stall, Tanvi hissed at him. I asked him to sit, poured him tea and showed him our numbers. He didn’t agree, but he took the petition to the meeting.
I’m not giving up on this. But if we lie about them, we lose our right to ask.
Hrithik

qa.q: Why does the library close at eight, according to Hrithik's letter?
qa.a: It closes at eight because of the electricity contract, not because of laziness.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel about the campaign after the poster row?
qa.a: Hrithik felt determined, saying he was not giving up, but he was firm that the campaign must stay truthful. He believed lying about the office would cost the group its right to ask.

qa.q: What choice made the meeting with Mr. Kulkarni useful?
qa.a: Hrithik invited him to sit, gave him tea and showed him the numbers instead of joining the hissing. Mr. Kulkarni still disagreed, but he took the petition to the meeting.

qa.q: How might Mr. Kulkarni have felt being hissed at and then given tea?
qa.a: He was probably startled and defensive at first, then a little disarmed by the courtesy. Taking the petition suggests he felt treated as a person rather than an enemy.

grounding: Shows a student volunteer staying firm on a cause while checking facts and treating the opposing office as human.

passage:
Samir, you asked how we kept it calm. Honestly, we didn’t always. I’m Kavitha, and our lane’s borewell was drying up, so forty of us went to the gate of the building site next door. Someone started shouting names at the site manager.
I stepped forward and said, “We’re here for the water, not against him.” Our placard claimed the site used ten times more than we did, and I asked who had checked. Nobody had. Rekha went to the municipal office the next morning, and the real figure was lower, though still large.
We reprinted the placard. Then the manager came out and listened for ten minutes. He said he would raise it. We hadn’t won, but people believed us after that.

qa.q: How many people went to the gate of the building site?
qa.a: Forty people went to the gate of the building site next door.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha step forward when someone started shouting names?
qa.a: Kavitha wanted the group to press its demand about the water without insulting the site manager. Kavitha's words, that they were there for the water, not against him, show a wish to keep the cause fair.

qa.q: What did the group do after finding the figure was wrong?
qa.a: They reprinted the placard with the correct, lower figure. That protected the group's credibility.

qa.q: How might the site manager have felt when the crowd stopped shouting and Kavitha spoke?
qa.a: He was probably wary at first, then more willing to listen, since he came out and listened for ten minutes. Being treated as a person rather than a target likely made that possible.

grounding: Shows a volunteer holding firm on a cause while treating an opponent as a person and correcting a wrong claim.

passage: I run the tea stall opposite the factory gate, so I saw the whole thing. For a month, Sudha and her college group had stood there every Saturday with placards about the black water in the canal. Some of the older protesters shouted 'Murderers!' at the workers going in. Sudha didn't. She said good morning to them, the same people every week. This Saturday the manager, Jagdish-ji, came out angry and said their pamphlet had the wrong numbers. Sudha asked to see his figures. She read them, standing right there, and said, 'You're right about this one. We'll correct it. But the canal is still black.' Jagdish-ji looked surprised. He accepted a cup of tea from me and stayed talking with her for half an hour. The next week, the new pamphlets had the corrected number. I don't know what will happen to the canal.

qa.q: What did some of the older protesters shout at the workers?
qa.a: 'Murderers!'

qa.q: How might Jagdish-ji have felt when Sudha admitted the mistake?
qa.a: Surprised and a little disarmed, since he came out angry and was met with honesty.

qa.q: What in Sudha's approach keeps the movement credible?
qa.a: She stays firm about the canal but checks the manager's figures, corrects the pamphlet and greets the workers as people.

qa.q: How might the workers going in see Sudha compared with the shouting protesters?
qa.a: They probably find Sudha easier to respect, since she greets them every week instead of calling them murderers.

grounding: A tea-stall owner's account of a young protester who stays firm on the cause while checking facts and treating opponents as people.

passage: Monday: Sunaina's campaign group for the street vendors of Park Road met in a café. Mahima showed a forwarded message: the ward officer had supposedly taken bribes from a mall developer. 'Let's post it tonight,' someone said. Sunaina hesitated. 'Do we have proof?' No one did. The group grumbled that she was being soft. Thursday: Sunaina called two vendors and a local journalist. The bribe story traced back to an anonymous account with no evidence. She told the group; Mahima admitted she'd been ready to post it. The following Monday: the group met the ward officer, Mr Deshmukh. Sunaina presented the vendors' real losses and a plan for fixed spots, and thanked him for his time. He didn't agree to everything, but he agreed to a second meeting.

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim about the ward officer?
qa.a: That he had taken bribes from a mall developer.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when the group called her soft?
qa.a: Sunaina felt uncomfortable and a bit alone, but steady in wanting proof before posting.

qa.q: Why did checking the bribe story protect the campaign?
qa.a: Posting an unproven claim would have cost the movement credibility; the checked facts let them meet Mr Deshmukh with real numbers.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel after learning the story was unproven?
qa.a: Embarrassed and relieved, having been ready to post it.

grounding: Over a week a young campaigner holds firm on the cause while insisting on facts and treating an official respectfully.

passage: Mohit, you're angry at the people who oppose your campaign? Let your Kalyani ajji tell you about 1986. The women of our village wanted the liquor shop near the school closed; men were drinking away their wages. We sat outside it every Sunday. Some women wanted to burn the shop down. I said no. The owner, Shankarappa, had children in the same school. So we sat outside singing, and I took him water when it was hot. Once our leaflet said he'd sold to children. He showed me his register; he hadn't. We printed a correction. People laughed at us for that. But when the district officer came, Shankarappa himself told him the women had been honest. The shop moved to the highway that year. Stay firm, Mohit. Just stay human.

qa.q: Where did the liquor shop move?
qa.a: To the highway.

qa.q: How might Shankarappa have felt when Kalyani brought him water in the heat?
qa.a: Surprised and perhaps touched, treated as a person even by those protesting his shop.

qa.q: Which choice in the story gave the women credibility?
qa.a: Checking Shankarappa's register and printing a correction when the leaflet was wrong, which led him to vouch for their honesty.

qa.q: How might the women who wanted to burn the shop have felt about Kalyani's stand?
qa.a: Frustrated at first, perhaps, but the peaceful, honest approach won in the end.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a village campaign that stayed firm while checking facts and treating the opponent as human.

passage: Two hours before the ward meeting, rain flooded the lane and the printer at the corner shop died. Jagdish and Sarita had forty leaflets to finish by hand, about the builder's plan to fence the old maidan. Sarita pushed her phone at him. "Look, a forward says the builder bribed the corporator. Put it on the leaflet. People will be furious." Jagdish read it twice. No source, no name. "If it's false, we lose everyone who trusts us," he said, and left it off. At the meeting the builder's manager, Mr Salve, spoke first, nervous, reading from a sheet. A man behind Jagdish shouted, "Thief!" Jagdish turned round. "He's doing his job. Let him finish." When his own turn came, he stuck to the map, the children's cricket matches, the rainwater that drains into the ground. Mr Salve nodded at a few points. Sarita, wet and cross, admitted afterwards, "They listened more than I expected."

qa.q: How many leaflets did Jagdish and Sarita have to finish by hand?
qa.a: They had forty leaflets to finish by hand.

qa.q: What was Jagdish worried about when he read the forward twice?
qa.a: He was worried that an unproven claim might be false and cost them the trust of everyone who believed in the campaign.

qa.q: Which of Jagdish's choices kept the campaign credible?
qa.a: He left out the unsourced claim, defended Mr Salve's right to speak, and stuck to facts like the map, the cricket matches and the drainage.

qa.q: How did Sarita see things by the end?
qa.a: She was wet and cross but admitted people listened more than she expected, so the careful approach surprised her.

grounding: Shows a volunteer staying firm on his cause while checking facts and treating the opponent's representative as a person.
